heading: Choosing plants and the guild
body: Choose plants that work together—and change the planting as it grows.

heading: Choosing plants and the guild
body: A fruit tree needs light, water, soil nutrients and space. Supporting plants can give food, leaves for mulch, flowers and a living cover.  Give each plant a useful job (the phrase 'umsebenzi oluncedo' has a concord slip). Keep checking whether it helps the tree and the home. Which functions does your planting need?

heading: Start with the site
body: Find out what is stopping growth before choosing a plant.

heading: Start with the site
body: Check sunlight, drainage (water coming out), soil condition and water availability. Nitrogen is only one of the things that can limit.  Compare the soil under mulch with soil that is not covered. Choose supporting plants that suit the existing conditions. What does this site need first?

heading: Give each plant a job
body: A useful guild produces benefits you can see.

heading: Give each plant a job
body: Choose members for food, putting in nitrogen, mulch, flowers or ground cover. One plant can do many jobs.  At the end, plan the guild, explain how plant residue feeds the soil, and decide which supporting plants you keep, cut or remove. Which job is not yet there?

heading: Look for root nodules
body: Legumes work together with rhizobia in the nodules on their roots.

heading: Look for root nodules
body: These bacteria change nitrogen in the air into the form (what) the legume can use.  Find nodules on an additional/extra legume plant. Nodule formation and growth depend on the plant, the right bacterium and the growing conditions. Can you find the nodules?

heading: Return the leaves to the soil
body: The nitrogen in plant material becomes useful as that material rots.

heading: Return the leaves to the soil
body: Return suitable leaf cuttings, fallen leaves and plant residue as mulch. Creatures that live in the soil release nutrients during rotting.  This takes time. A living legume is not a pump of quick fertiliser going to the fruit tree. Which residue can you return?

heading: Sesbania has a useful role
body: Sesbania sesban can give fast growth and leaves for mulch.

heading: Sesbania has a useful role
body: It is native to KwaZulu-Natal. In suitable warm conditions, manage this shrub or short-lived small tree as a supporting plant.  Leave it a place to grow. Cut it to get mulch and check it again when shade or water competition goes up. Where can you manage its growth?

heading: Check the full name of the plant
body: Sesbania sesban and Sesbania punicea are different kinds.

heading: Check the full name of the plant
body: Sesbania punicea is a red sesbania that invades uncontrollably. Its pods have four wings, nearly (the) length ('aphantse ubude'). Confirm which plant it is using a trusted plant guide.  Check the full name before planting. Respect the project's approved species list, including any restriction on Sesbania sesban. Can the seller confirm which plant it is?

heading: Pigeon pea also gives food
body: Pigeon pea—Cajanus cajan—can give peas, leaf material and putting in nitrogen.

heading: Pigeon pea also gives food
body: Use a sunny place, where water goes up/rises freely (reads as water 'rising', not draining). It is a short-lived supporting shrub; frost and waterlogged soil can hold it back.  Decide whether each plant mainly gives peas or leaf material. Cutting too much, often, can harm the plant and reduce the food harvest. Are you planting this plant to harvest peas or to get mulch?

heading: Choose by site and size
body: A supporting tree that is useful in one place can be too big or unsuitable in another.

heading: Choose by site and size
body: Compare crown, roots, shade, rain and heat when it is already grown. Check the species suited to your site and the planting rules.  Put big supporting trees where there is room. In a small young guild, a manageable shrub may be easier to keep. How big will this plant be?

heading: A seasonal cover has its place
body: Sunn hemp can cover (a) suitable warm-season patch/bed before the next crop (the verb form 'inganigqubuthela' is garbled).

heading: A seasonal cover has its place
body: Plant it where its season and place agree with the plan. Its contribution depends on growth, nodule making and the material returned.  After cutting, leave time for rotting. A yearly cover plant has a different role from a long-living supporting shrub. When will this place be needed again?

heading: Leave space around the tree
body: Keep the young fruit tree lit (with light) and leave an access way so you can look after it.

heading: Leave space around the tree
body: Keep the establishment basin open, and the path to the fruit tree. Place short-term supporting plants where their size and use of water can be controlled.  Place leaf cuttings where mulch is needed. Neighbouring fruit trees can share supporter lines between them. Can you reach both plants as they grow?

heading: Build a supporting guild with layers
body: Combine the seasonal cover, supporting shrubs and short-lived small trees.

heading: Build a supporting guild with layers
body: Cowpea covers sunny patches. Pigeon pea gives food and leaf material. A managed Sesbania sesban can give tall short-term support.  Add suitable flowering plants and mulch plants. Keep the mango trunk clean and manage light, water and access. Which layers suit your site?

heading: How many supporting plants?
body: Plan much support where your space and care can support it.

heading: How many supporting plants?
body: Count the woody supporters across the whole area between the fruit trees. Sow ground cover suitable for the size of the area.  No single number works for every fruit tree. Adjust the crowding by water, soil, plant size and your ability to cut and thin. How much support can you keep?

heading: Chop-and-drop for light and mulch
body: Watch a branch fall over cut leaves.

heading: Chop-and-drop for light and mulch
body: Chop the supporting tree and return suitable leaf cuttings to the soil. The clip shows the cutting of a branch: the supporting tree remains standing. Leave enough healthy leaves so that the plant can recover again.  Match the cutting to the kind of plant. Avoid cutting too much, often, on pigeon pea, especially when you plant it to harvest peas. Which plant needs cutting—and how much?

heading: Keep mulch away from the stem
body: Spread suitable cut material over the soil, the stem and root neck left clean.

heading: Keep mulch away from the stem
body: Mulch protects the surface, helps keep moisture and returns organic material.  Leave a way for watering and checking. Cut the material into manageable pieces and keep checking moisture and rotting. Is the root neck still clean?

heading: Choose the correct comfrey
body: Bocking 14 comfrey can give cut leaves for mulch.

heading: Choose the correct comfrey
body: Find the suitable variety (cultivar). Bocking 14 does not spread by seed that is able to germinate, but root pieces can sprout again.  Place it where it has space and enough moisture. Cut leaves as it grows again; do not crowd/squeeze the young fruit tree. Is this a good permanent place for this comfrey group?

heading: Look for helpful insects
body: Flowers can provide resources (tools) for helpful insects.

heading: Look for helpful insects
body: Many ladybirds eat aphids; some parasitoid wasps attack insects that damage plants. Flowering members such as African basil can add resources.  Look at which insects visit and whether the damage changes. A flowering plant does not guarantee pest control. What is the insect actually doing?

heading: Give flowers their place
body: Wild garlic can be a flowering member where the place suits it.

heading: Give flowers their place
body: Tulbaghia violacea has narrow/crowded(?) leaves ('amxinwa') and lilac flowers. Place the group where it can get light and room to grow.  Watch for visiting insects. Do not promise that a circle/cycle of wild garlic will drive away pests or cure their outbreak. Where can the flowers grow without crowding?

heading: Combine jobs
body: Choose helpful partners while protecting the growing space of the mango.

heading: Combine jobs
body: Combine the support jobs your site needs: putting in nitrogen, food, mulch, flowers and ground cover. Some plants do many jobs.  Keep the stem area and the path open. Check each member again as the mango and its neighbours grow. Does each member have space and a job?

heading: Food ground cover also competes
body: Sweet potato can cover the soil and give food in a suitable sunny place.

heading: Food ground cover also competes
body: Keep its creeping stems away from the young fruit tree and keep the way for care. Its roots also use water and nutrients.  Where resources are scarce, compare the living cover with an ordinary mulch basin. Does this cover help the tree to become established?

heading: First, establish the guild
body: Start while the young fruit tree and its supporting plants can have enough light and water.

heading: First, establish the guild
body: Plant at a suitable time, cover with mulch and give establishment water. Keep the access space open.  Start with the number of supporting plants you can look after. Check survival and growth before adding others. Can you look after all the plants during establishment?

heading: Thin as the fruit tree grows
body: When chopping/pruning is no longer enough, reduce selected supporting plants. Cut down selected competing supporters to open space. Suitable cut material can stay as mulch: this is thinning by chop-and-drop.  Manage regrowth to keep the place open. Check light, soil moisture and growth; thinning does not stop root competition immediately. Which supporting plants must now give up space?

heading: Move support toward the light
body: As shade increases, renew sun-loving supporting plants on the open sides and in new planting.

heading: Move support toward the light
body: Take useful cuttings and return them to established trees. Keep only nearby plants where they are doing well.  A mature fruit tree still needs nutrients. Check growth, harvest and soil conditions; supporting plants do not remove that need. Where is the next useful sunny place?

heading: Let what you see decide
body: Keep a short record of how the guild works.

heading: Let what you see decide
body: Check fruit tree growth, shade, soil moisture, useful harvests and pest damage. Write what was cut, returned or removed.  Use what you have seen to change the design and care. A plant deserves its place by performing here. What little evidence could make you change the guild?

heading: Plan one real guild
body: Choose one fruit tree (and) mark a design you can manage.

heading: Plan one real guild
body: Record the tree, site conditions and the functions not yet there. Describe the supporting plants with the full name, mark the starting number and leave an access way.  Write down what will cause cutting or thinning. Agree with the species list and the project team where necessary. Can someone else explain your plan to you again?

heading: Plant, watch, adjust
body: Start one suitable guild and look after it in its first stage.

heading: Plant, watch, adjust
body: Use the correct kind, a manageable number of plants and a growing place. Return useful plant material to protect the fruit tree.  Review the planting as the crowns have spread. Keep, cut, change or remove each supporting plant when its role changes. What will you do first—and when will you check it?
